title: Perceiving Compliance in Virtual Reality: Effects of Interaction Direction and Sensory Discrepancy on Visuo-Haptic Weighting
venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
imageAlt: Haptic and visual stiffness rendering with baseline, top-down, front-back, and side-to-side VR interaction configurations
summary: When a virtual object looks softer than it feels, the direction of the press can change which cue a person trusts. The effect depends on how far apart the visual and haptic cues are.
abstract: In Virtual Reality (VR), users judge object compliance by combining visually displayed deformation with physically delivered force, yet it remains unclear whether both modalities require equally high rendering fidelity across interaction conditions, particularly when rendering resources are limited. We investigated visuo-haptic weighting in compliance perception across interaction directions and visuo-haptic discrepancy magnitudes. Two discrepancy magnitudes were tested across three representative interaction directions: a smaller magnitude comparable to values commonly used in sensory-weighting studies and a larger magnitude that remained perceptually acceptable in VR. Under the larger discrepancy, visual influence was greater in vertical top-down interaction, whereas haptic influence was greater in front-back interaction, while side-to-side interaction showed more balanced weighting. Directional effects were minimal under the smaller discrepancy. Together, these findings suggest that compliance rendering in VR may benefit from accounting for interaction direction, rather than assuming a single uniform visuo-haptic balance across interaction conditions.
contribution: The study separates two factors that can change a compliance judgment: the direction of the hand movement and the size of the mismatch between deformation and force.
results: When pressing downward, participants relied more on visible deformation. In front-to-back movements, they relied more on force. Side-to-side judgments were more balanced. These differences were small when the cues agreed more closely, suggesting that rendering fidelity can be allocated according to the interaction.

title: CineHaptic: Context-Aware Real-Time Audiovisual-to-Haptic Rendering System for In-Vehicle 4D Cinematic Experiences
venue: ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology
booktitle: Proceedings of the 39th Annual ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology
imageAlt: CineHaptic pipeline from audiovisual event localization, salience classification, and audio processing to seat-based haptic patterns for an in-car 4D experience
summary: CineHaptic turns an action scene into vibrations a passenger can feel through a car seat. It works during playback without a manually authored haptic track.
abstract: Haptic feedback significantly enriches cinematic experiences, but existing manual authoring and offline generation methods lack the scalability required for rapidly growing streaming media libraries. To address this, we present CineHaptic, a real-time system that automatically generates haptic effects by extracting the semantic context of audiovisual media for immersive in-vehicle 4D experiences. For each sound event, the system classifies its semantic salience into a four-level hierarchy, determining the necessity and intensity of haptic actuation. Concurrently, a cross-modal audiovisual analysis module estimates the sound’s spatial origin in the scene. CineHaptic then seamlessly synthesizes this semantic and spatial data into coherent spatiotemporal patterns, delivered through a custom six-actuator haptic seat. System-level evaluations confirm strict adherence to real-time processing and multisensory synchrony requirements over full-length cinematic content. Furthermore, an in-car user study demonstrates that haptic feedback integrating semantic salience, spatial location, and temporal dynamics significantly enhances user immersion and preference compared to baseline methods. Ultimately, CineHaptic provides a fully automated, scalable pipeline for high-fidelity multisensory rendering, tailored for next-generation in-vehicle entertainment.
contribution: CineHaptic assigns each sound event a salience level, locates its source in the image and maps its timing and intensity to six actuators in a car seat. The system generates a haptic track during playback, without requiring an author to annotate each scene.
results: In a parked vehicle, 28 participants compared four rendering methods. Filtering low-salience sounds reduced distracting vibrations. Matching the seat vibration to the event’s on-screen location produced the highest immersion and preference ratings. A full-length playback test also showed that the system could keep the seat feedback synchronized.

title: Representing Egocentric Directions with Torso-Applied Vibrotactile Stimuli
imageAlt: Torso-based vibrotactile display for azimuth and elevation cues
summary: How can vibrations on the torso communicate directions in 3D space? Four perceptual experiments connect tactile locations to perceived azimuth and elevation.
abstract: This paper investigates egocentric directional perception of azimuth and elevation in response to torso-based vibrotactile stimuli for both stimulus identification and direction association under a common experimental framework. We conducted four perceptual experiments that examined the two tasks for azimuth and elevation, using real vibrations and illusory stimuli generated by the funneling illusion. The results demonstrated that adding illusory stimuli effectively conveyed directional information with fewer tactors than using only real stimuli. Azimuth perception revealed a lateral bias, whereas elevation perception exhibited a downward bias on the dorsal torso, particularly in the upper back. However, both azimuth and elevation cues were generally consistent across vertical and horizontal torso locations. Additionally, we estimated regression models for both egocentric angles and showed that perceived directions could be estimated from actual stimulus positions. Correlation analysis revealed a weak relationship between azimuth and elevation perceptual errors, suggesting that these dimensions are processed with near-independence. Across all findings, azimuth cues proved to be more effective than elevation cues in conveying directional information. This study provides a comprehensive understanding of egocentric directions and offers practical insights for the design of torso-based vibrotactile displays.
contribution: Four experiments distinguish recognizing a location on the skin from associating that location with a direction in space. The resulting regression models map stimulation sites to perceived azimuth and elevation for both physical and illusory vibration locations.
results: Azimuth judgments tended toward the sides, and vibrations high on the back felt lower than their intended elevation. Errors in the two dimensions were only weakly related. Azimuth cues conveyed direction more effectively overall. The measured biases can guide placement when a vest must point toward a particular angle.

title: Human Identification Performance of Vibrotactile Stimuli Applied on the Torso Along Azimuth or Elevation
booktitle: Haptics: Understanding Touch; Technology and Systems; Applications and Interaction
imageAlt: Experimental torso layouts for identifying azimuth and elevation stimuli
summary: Measuring how accurately people identify horizontal and vertical tactile locations, and what happens when illusory stimuli double the available positions.
abstract: This study investigates the human recognition performance of vibrotactile stimuli applied on the torso along azimuth or elevation under the context of tactile egocentric directional cueing. We conducted two absolute identification experiments for azimuth and elevation, respectively, using real tactile stimuli generated by physical actuators and illusory stimuli rendered by funneling illusion. For both azimuth and elevation, the recognition accuracies were very high, over 95.6%, when only real stimuli were used to indicate 6-8 directions. However, combining the real stimuli with the illusory ones to double the spatial resolution resulted in significantly lower accuracies between 74.1% and 77.8%. The estimated information transfer (IT) values also remained very similar. Using identical methods, our results quantify the human identification performance of torso-distributed tactile stimuli for azimuth or elevation. The detailed results provide general guidelines for designing torso-based tactile systems to enhance spatial awareness and navigation.
contribution: Two matched experiments compare horizontal and vertical cue identification on the torso. Adding apparent vibration locations between adjacent motors makes it possible to test twice as many positions with the same hardware.
results: With physical locations alone, participants identified six to eight directions with over 95.6% accuracy. Doubling the number of positions with illusory cues reduced accuracy to 74.1–77.8%, with little change in estimated information transfer. A vest can therefore offer finer spacing without necessarily conveying more distinguishable information.

title: Telemetry-Based Haptic Rendering for Racing Game Experience Improvement
imageAlt: Telemetry-based haptic rendering pipeline and racing simulator
summary: Turning racing-game telemetry into tactile engine, collision, and road effects, with independent control over each part of the driving experience.
abstract: Many recent games, such as racing and flight games, open their game telemetry data to users by storing them in the local memory. Such telemetry data can provide useful information for haptic rendering, and this advantage has been exploited by the industry. This approach applies to any applications that export telemetry data in run time. The haptic rendering module operates as a separate process that accesses the telemetry data in parallel with the application. It is simple, efficient, and modular while retaining the application intact. We examine the approach’s viability for user experience improvement by developing three telemetry-based haptic rendering algorithms for car racing games. They express the car engine response, collisions with external objects, and the road surface texture, respectively. Building a haptics-enabled driving platform, we conducted a user study comparing gaming experiences between our telemetry-based algorithms and conventional sound-to-tactile conversion algorithms. The results showed that the telemetry-based effects elicited better experiences than the sound-based effects.
contribution: Three rendering algorithms translate engine response, impacts and road texture into independently adjustable vibrations. A separate process reads the game telemetry and drives the simulator, so the game itself needs no modification.
results: Participants rated the telemetry-driven effects more favorably overall than effects derived from game audio. Separating the three sources lets designers tune the feel of a collision without also changing the engine or road vibration. The comparison was against sound-based methods and did not rank commercial telemetry systems.

title: Information Transfer of Full-Body Vibrotactile Stimuli: An Initial Study with One to Three Sequential Vibrations
imageAlt: Full-body vibrotactile stimulation and sequential vibration patterns
summary: Quantifying how much information people can distinguish when one, two, or three vibrations are delivered in sequence across the body.
abstract: Full-body vibrotactile stimuli are a promising means by which haptic interaction designers can substantially increase information transfer (IT). This paper reports the IT values of full-body sequential vibrotactile stimuli applied to ten body sites. We designed 10, 100, and 1,000 stimuli by increasing the number of vibrations in a sequence from one to three and estimated IT for each condition. We also obtained the lower and upper bounds of the IT estimates using several empirical methods to compensate for their biases. The IT estimate for each condition was 3.32, 6.55, and 8.05 bits, the highest IT ever reported in the haptics literature. This study is the first attempt to quantify the IT of full-body vibrotactile sequences, providing guidelines for the design of effective full-body vibrotactile stimuli.
contribution: The study varies sequence length while holding the set of ten stimulation sites fixed. It compares empirical estimates and their bounds to measure information transfer even when three vibrations produce 1,000 possible sequences.
results: Estimated information transfer rose from 3.32 bits for one vibration to 6.55 for two and 8.05 for three. The third vibration increased capacity, but by less than the second. These estimates give designers a basis for choosing how many successive body locations to use for a tactile message.

title: Human Recognition Performance of Simple Spatial Vibrotactile Patterns on the Torso
imageAlt: Haptic vest and spatial vibration patterns on the front, back, and horizontal torso
summary: Investigating which simultaneous vibration patterns people can recognize on the torso, toward a practical vocabulary for haptic vests.
abstract: This paper presents an experimental study on the fundamental human recognition performance of spatial tactile patterns applied on the torso. The patterns are made by either activating or deactivating four vibration actuators fastened to the body surface in a rectangular shape. Three body areas are considered for stimulation: the torso’s front (chest and stomach), back, and waist. A perceptual experiment shows that the human recognition accuracy of the spatial tactile patterns is high on the torso, over 91%. The accuracy depends on the stimulated body area and the number of simultaneously activated vibrations. In addition, the estimated information transfer ranges from 3.48 bits to 3.66 bits, indicating that the torso can transmit 11–12 spatial patterns without errors. These results can contribute to designing spatial tactile patterns that are effective for recently emerging haptic vests.
contribution: The experiments test all 16 on/off patterns of four actuators at three torso locations. Confusion matrices identify which simultaneous patterns can serve as distinct signals in a haptic vest.
results: Mean recognition was about 95% on the front and back and 91% around the waist. Estimated information transfer was 3.48–3.66 bits, equivalent to roughly 11–12 perfectly distinguishable patterns. Both the layout and the number of motors activated at once affected recognition.
